name: E-Commerce Inventory System
description: Design an inventory management system for e-commerce at scale. Covers stock tracking, reservation-based checkout, cache consistency, oversell prevention, and async stock replenishment.

learnSteps.title: Stock Level Reads with Cache-Aside
learnSteps.description: Product listing pages need sub-10ms stock level checks. The Inventory Service first checks Redis for stock counts (98% hit rate). On cache miss, it queries PostgreSQL and populates Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Stock levels in Redis are approximate for reads (eventual consistency is acceptable for display), but writes use a different path to ensure accuracy. This pattern handles flash sale traffic spikes.

learnSteps.title: Atomic Stock Reservation (Oversell Prevention)
learnSteps.description: When a user adds to cart or checks out, the Inventory Service uses Redis DECRBY atomically to reserve stock. If the result is negative, the reservation fails immediately (no oversell). The service then publishes a reservation event to Kafka. This two-phase approach uses Redis for speed and atomicity, while PostgreSQL maintains the source of truth. The noeviction policy ensures stock counters are never lost.

learnSteps.title: Reservation Confirmation and Expiry
learnSteps.description: The Reservation Worker consumes events from Kafka and confirms the reservation in PostgreSQL using a serializable transaction (UPDATE stock SET available = available - quantity WHERE available >= quantity). If the DB transaction succeeds, the reservation is confirmed. Unconfirmed reservations expire after 15 minutes, and the worker releases the Redis counter via INCRBY. This prevents cart-holding attacks.

learnSteps.title: Cache-Database Consistency
learnSteps.description: After DB writes (order confirmed, stock replenished, reservation expired), the Worker invalidates the Redis key rather than updating it, avoiding stale cache issues. The next read triggers a cache-aside refill from PostgreSQL. For hot products during flash sales, Redis counters are treated as authoritative and periodically synced to PostgreSQL via batch reconciliation, trading consistency for throughput.

chaosScenarios.name: Redis Counter Loss
chaosScenarios.description: The stock cache crashes and loses the authoritative reservation counters that gate every checkout
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Reservations must fail closed: with counters gone, any DECRBY against a missing key risks overselling. Checkout success rate drops to zero (or falls back to slow serializable DB transactions at a fraction of the throughput) until counters are rebuilt from PostgreSQL plus unexpired reservations.
mitigationSteps: Fail reservations closed when a counter key is absent — never default to 'in stock'
Fail over to the Redis replica; verify AOF/RDB persistence before readmitting traffic
Rebuild counters from PostgreSQL available stock minus unexpired reservations, then re-enable checkout per SKU

chaosScenarios.name: Flash Sale Hot-SKU Stampede
chaosScenarios.description: A promoted product launches and a single SKU receives 50x normal reservation traffic concentrated on one Redis key
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: All DECRBY operations for the SKU serialize on one Redis core; command latency climbs from sub-ms to tens of ms, app-server threads block on cache calls, and p99 checkout latency blows past 1s while unrelated SKUs degrade as collateral.
mitigationSteps: Shard the hot SKU's counter across N sub-counters and rebalance remainders
Put a checkout queue in front of the SKU so admission is throttled instead of timing out
Serve display-only stock levels from a short-TTL local cache to take reads off the hot key

chaosScenarios.name: Reservation Worker Stall
chaosScenarios.description: All reservation workers crash (bad deploy), so Kafka events stop being confirmed in PostgreSQL
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Events accumulate safely in Kafka (168h retention), but DB confirmations and the reservation-expiry sweeper stop. Redis counters stay decremented past the 15-minute window, so items appear sold out while PostgreSQL still shows stock — drift grows linearly with lag.
mitigationSteps: Roll back the worker deploy and restart the consumer group
Scale workers up to the partition count to drain the backlog
Run the reconciliation job to release expired reservations and re-sync Redis with PostgreSQL

bottleneckProgression.description: Cache-miss reads plus worker confirmations exhaust the 300-connection PostgreSQL pool
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add PgBouncer transaction pooling and route stock-level reads to replicas

bottleneckProgression.description: Atomic counter operations concentrate on popular SKUs and saturate the single-threaded Redis core
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Shard counters per SKU across cluster slots; move display reads to a local cache tier

bottleneckProgression.description: 16 partitions cap consumer parallelism while reservation events outpace worker throughput
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Increase partition count and scale the reservation worker group to match

expectedIssues.title: Oversell from Cache–DB Drift
expectedIssues.description: Duplicate Kafka delivery, counter rebuild errors, or missed invalidations let Redis report more stock than PostgreSQL actually has
expectedIssues.mitigation: Keep the conditional UPDATE (WHERE available >= quantity) as the final guard, make reservation IDs idempotent, and run continuous drift reconciliation

expectedIssues.title: Hot-SKU Counter Contention
expectedIssues.description: Flash-sale traffic concentrates on a single Redis key, hitting the per-key throughput ceiling long before cluster capacity
expectedIssues.mitigation: Pre-shard counters for promoted SKUs and front the checkout with an admission queue

expectedIssues.title: Phantom Inventory from Abandoned Carts
expectedIssues.description: Reservations that never convert hold stock for the full 15-minute window, deflating apparent availability during peaks
expectedIssues.mitigation: Keep the expiry sweeper aggressive, release via INCRBY promptly, and shorten the hold window during flash sales

expectedIssues.title: Confirmation Contention on Popular SKU Rows
expectedIssues.description: Serializable confirmation transactions for the same SKU contend on one row, raising serialization failures and retry load
expectedIssues.mitigation: Batch confirmations per SKU inside the worker and partition Kafka by SKU so one worker owns each row

expectedIssues.title: Consumer Rebalance Duplicate Processing
expectedIssues.description: Worker restarts trigger Kafka rebalances; redelivered events can double-confirm or double-release a reservation
expectedIssues.mitigation: Idempotency keys per reservation and a processed-event table checked inside the confirmation transaction

components.label: API Gateway
components.costDriver: Gateway instances + request volume at 30k RPS

slaDefinitions.name: Oversell Rate
slaDefinitions.penalty: Full refund + goodwill credit per oversold order

metrics.name: reservation_success_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of reservation attempts admitted by the Redis counter

metrics.name: stock_counter_drift
metrics.description: Absolute difference between Redis counters and PostgreSQL stock found by reconciliation

metrics.name: kafka_consumer_lag
metrics.description: Unconfirmed reservation events pending in the queue

metrics.name: serialization_failures
metrics.description: PostgreSQL confirmation transactions aborted by row contention

metrics.name: cache_hit_rate
metrics.description: Stock read hit rate against the 98% target

steps: Confirm checkout is failing closed — no reservations admitted without a counter
Snapshot Kafka consumer offsets before any rebuild
Rebuild counters from PostgreSQL available stock minus unexpired reservations
Re-enable checkout SKU-by-SKU while watching the drift metric
Run full reconciliation and audit orders placed in the failure window
Check worker health and recent deploys; roll back if the stall followed a release
Scale the consumer group toward the partition count
Inspect for a poison message if one partition lags alone
Verify the expiry sweeper is releasing stale reservations as lag drains
Pause sales for the affected SKU immediately
Quantify oversold orders from the reconciliation report
Correct Redis counters and PostgreSQL stock, then re-enable sales
Trigger the customer-care flow for affected orders and file a postmortem

decisions.title: Redis Atomic Counters as the Reservation Gate
decisions.context: Flash sales push thousands of concurrent reservations at a single SKU; row-locked database transactions serialize on that row
decisions.decision: Admit or reject every reservation with an atomic DECRBY against a per-SKU Redis counter, failing immediately on a negative result
consequences: Reservation decisions in ~1ms with no row contention
Counters become operationally critical state requiring noeviction, persistence, and a rebuild procedure

decisions.title: Async Confirmation Through Kafka
decisions.context: Durable confirmation in PostgreSQL does not need to block the checkout response
decisions.decision: Publish reservation events to Kafka and confirm in the database via workers using a conditional UPDATE (WHERE available >= quantity)
consequences: Checkout latency stays decoupled from database write load
A bounded drift window exists where Redis and PostgreSQL disagree, requiring reconciliation

decisions.title: Invalidate-on-Write Cache Consistency
decisions.context: Concurrent writers updating cached stock values race and can persist stale data
decisions.decision: Workers delete the Redis display key after database writes instead of writing through
consequences: No stale-write races between concurrent updaters
The first read after invalidation pays a database round trip

tradeoffs.choice: Two-tier counters: Redis fast path, PostgreSQL source of truth
tradeoffs.benefit: Flash-sale reservation throughput far beyond what single-row DB locking allows
tradeoffs.cost: Drift between tiers must be continuously detected and reconciled

tradeoffs.benefit: Carts cannot hold stock hostage and cart-holding attacks are bounded
tradeoffs.cost: Slow shoppers occasionally lose items mid-checkout

alternatives.name: Serializable DB Transactions Only
alternatives.description: Every reservation runs a serializable transaction directly against PostgreSQL with no cache fast path
alternatives.prosVsCons: Correct by construction with zero drift, but row-lock contention caps a hot SKU at a few hundred reservations per second
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Cannot survive flash-sale concurrency on popular SKUs

alternatives.name: Distributed Lock per SKU
alternatives.description: Acquire a lock, read stock, decide, write, release for each reservation
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simple mental model, but adds lock-service round trips and creates a serialization point per SKU anyway
alternatives.whyNotChosen: An atomic counter gives the same admission guarantee in a single Redis operation
